# How to Find Your Google Meet Recordings, Transcripts and Notes

> **In short:** Google Meet saves recordings, transcripts, and Gemini-written notes into the meeting organizer's Google Drive, inside a folder called **Meet Recordings**. Attendees get a link by email. If you can't find a file, you probably weren't the person who scheduled the meeting.

You've just stepped out of a 45-minute call, your manager told everyone to "check the recording afterwards", and now you're staring at Google Drive wondering where the file went. It isn't lost — it just lives in a specific spot. Here's how to actually find it, every time.

## Before you start

You'll need:

- A Google account (personal Gmail or Google Workspace — the paid version most schools and businesses use).
- **Recording** and **"Take notes for me"** features generally require a **Google Workspace** plan. Some personal accounts have access, but it's not guaranteed.
- A meeting that's already been recorded, transcribed, or noted by Gemini.

If you're not sure which account you used, check the email address on the meeting invite. The organizer is usually the person who sent the calendar invitation — that's the Drive where the files will land.

## Step 1 — Find the meeting organizer's folder in Drive

Open **Google Drive** (drive.google.com) and sign in with the same account that scheduled the meeting. On the left sidebar, click **My Drive**. Scroll or search for a folder named after the organizer — for work, this is often a shared drive or a folder with the meeting owner's name.

You'll know it worked when you see a folder called **Meet Recordings** inside it.

💬 **Example search:** In the Drive search bar, type `Meet Recordings` and filter by **Folders**. The organizer-specific folder should appear.

## Step 2 — Open the correct meeting inside Meet Recordings

Click into **Meet Recordings**. Each meeting gets its own subfolder, usually named with the meeting title and date. Open the one that matches your meeting.

You'll know it worked when you see three items inside: an **MP4 video file**, a **Google Docs transcript**, and a **Google Docs notes file** (when those features were turned on).

💬 **Example file names:** `Meet Recording - Weekly Sync - 2026-03-04.mp4`, `Transcript - Weekly Sync`, `Notes - Weekly Sync`.

## Step 3 — Play the recording in your browser

Double-click the **MP4 file**. Google Drive will open a built-in video player in your browser — no download required. You can scrub through the timeline, adjust playback speed, and share the file with a link.

You'll know it worked when the video loads and the timeline shows the meeting's full duration.

💬 **Tip:** Right-click the file → **Open with → Google Drive video player** if it doesn't auto-play.

## Step 4 — Read the transcript file

Back in the meeting folder, double-click the **Transcript** Google Doc. It opens in your browser like any other Google Doc. The transcript is generated automatically once the meeting ends, so it may take a few minutes to appear.

You'll know it worked when you see speaker labels and timestamped lines of what each person said.

💬 **Example line:** `[00:12:34] Sarah: Let's revisit the budget for Q2.`

## Step 5 — Open the Gemini-written meeting notes

In the same folder, double-click the **Notes** Google Doc. This file is written by **Gemini** (Google's AI assistant) *after* the meeting ends, summarizing the key points discussed.

You'll know it worked when you see a short summary at the top, followed by bulleted action items and decisions.

💬 **Example line:** `Key decision: Postpone the March launch to April 15. Owner: Priya.`

## Step 6 — Find the link if you were an attendee, not the organizer

If you joined the meeting but didn't schedule it, the files won't appear in your Drive. Instead, check the **email inbox** linked to the Google account you used to join. The organizer (or Google itself) sends a message with subject lines like *"Recording ready: [Meeting title]"*. Open that email and click the attached link.

You'll know it worked when clicking the link opens the same recording in your browser — and you can request access if the file is private.

💬 **Tip:** Can't find the email? Open **Google Calendar**, find the meeting event, and scroll down — the recording link is often attached to the event details.

## Common mistakes

- **Looking in your own Drive for a meeting you didn't schedule.** The files go to the organizer's Drive, not yours. Fix: ask the organizer to share the folder with you, or use the email link method.
- **Assuming the recording didn't save because you don't see it immediately.** Google Meet takes a few minutes to process the file after the meeting ends. Fix: refresh Drive after 5-10 minutes, or check the email link.
- **Turning on "Take notes for me" but expecting notes during the call.** Gemini writes the summary *after* the meeting ends, not in real time. Fix: wait until you get the email confirmation, then check the Notes file in the same Drive folder.
- **Using a personal Gmail account and wondering why recording is missing.** The feature is often locked to Workspace plans. Fix: ask your IT admin (for work) or check Google's support page for personal-account availability.
- **Closing the meeting before the transcript finishes generating.** The file can fail to save if you exit too quickly. Fix: stay on the "meeting ended" screen for at least 30 seconds, or wait for the email confirmation that processing is complete.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life**: if you use Meet for a book club, a family catch-up, or a study group, the simplest habit is to **always check your email after a meeting**. The recording link lands there, even if you forget where you saved it.
- **For your work or business**: nominate one person per recurring meeting to be the **organizer on the calendar invite**. Recordings will then always land in *their* Drive, and everyone else can rely on the email link. It saves the "where do we keep recordings?" question for good.
- **If you're just getting started**: try recording your next short Google Meet. Then open Drive, navigate to your meeting owner's folder, and look for the **Meet Recordings** subfolder. Once you've seen the layout once, it's obvious.
- **If a recording seems missing**: check the organizer's Drive first, then the email link, then the Calendar event attachment — in that order. One of those three will have it.
